title: Memory Evolution — Memory Hierarchy and SOTA

topics.title: Von Neumann Architecture and the Memory Wall

notes.title: Von Neumann fetch-and-execute workflow and separation of memory and processing unit
notes.summary: 冯·诺依曼架构将存储器与处理单元分离，按取指、执行、写回的流程工作，而处理单元执行指令的速度远快于访存，形成内存墙瓶颈。
notes.detail: 工作流为：从存储器取指令和数据，在ALU上执行指令，再把计算结果写回存储器。由于PU执行指令比内存访问快几个数量级，这种分离结构导致内存墙。
keyPoints: 取指、执行、写回构成基本循环
存储器与处理单元物理分离
PU速度远超访存速度，形成瓶颈

notes.title: Processor-DRAM performance gap growing ~50% per year
notes.summary: 处理器与DRAM之间的性能差距历史上以每年约50%的速度扩大，因此仅靠更快的处理器并不能保证应用更快。
notes.detail: 该50%差距描述的是图中所示历史时期的趋势。处理器性能提升并不能自动转化为应用性能提升，因为数据供给跟不上。
keyPoints: 性能差距年增长约50%
该比例对应图中历史时期
更快的处理器不等于更快的应用

notes.title: Scaling laws meet memory walls (LLM scaling, post-Dennard scaling of AI workloads)
notes.summary: LLM规模扩展与AI加速器的后Dennard扩展共同撞上内存墙：模型参数、数据和推理链变长，而Tensor Core吞吐增长远快于HBM容量。
notes.detail: LLM扩展带来参数与数据量增加、思维链长度与搜索深度增加，模型规模与上下文更大。同时AI加速器的Tensor Core吞吐增长远快于HBM容量，使内存墙在AI负载中进一步加宽。
keyPoints: LLM参数、数据与推理链持续增长
Tensor Core吞吐增速超过HBM容量增速
内存墙在AI加速器上被进一步拉宽

notes.title: Memory capacity per core declining as cores double faster than DRAM capacity
notes.summary: 处理核心数约每两年翻倍，而DRAM DIMM容量约每三年才翻倍，导致每核内存容量预计每两年下降30%。
notes.detail: 核心数翻倍速度快于DRAM容量翻倍速度，使每核可用内存容量持续萎缩，大量数据可能不得不从低速磁盘加载。
keyPoints: 核心数约2年翻倍，DRAM容量约3年翻倍
每核容量预计每两年降30%
数据可能回落到低速磁盘

notes.title: Capacity, bandwidth, and latency dimensions of the memory wall
notes.summary: 内存墙体现在容量、带宽和延迟三个维度上，且带宽与延迟的趋势都在恶化。
notes.detail: 该页以容量、带宽和延迟三个维度刻画内存墙。图中趋势表明带宽和延迟的表现都在变差。
keyPoints: 内存墙包含容量、带宽、延迟三个维度
带宽与延迟趋势均在恶化

notes.title: Role of main memory in retaining programs and data across computing systems
notes.summary: 主存是所有计算系统（服务器、移动、嵌入式、桌面、传感器）的关键部件，存储跨运行保留程序与数据，主存则保存可供活跃执行的部分。
notes.detail: 存储负责跨运行保留程序和数据，主存只保存其中可供活跃执行的部分。缓存则在执行单元附近保留副本，减少从主存的传输。
keyPoints: 主存适用于各类计算系统
存储跨运行保留，主存保存活跃执行部分
缓存减少主存传输

notes.title: Main memory in FPGA-based systems
notes.summary: FPGA将逻辑块及其连接配置为特定任务的电路，片上SRAM（如block RAM）在处理逻辑附近缓冲输入和中间结果。
notes.detail: FPGA针对特定任务配置逻辑块与互连形成电路。片上SRAM（如block RAM）在处理逻辑附近缓冲输入与中间结果，起到靠近计算的数据暂存作用。
keyPoints: FPGA按任务配置逻辑块与连接
block RAM等片上SRAM缓冲输入与中间结果
片上存储靠近处理逻辑

notes.title: Discrete GPU device memory as part of the main memory system
notes.summary: 独立GPU使用自己的设备DRAM（GDDR芯片或HBM堆栈），计算结果可留在设备内存供下次计算使用，或在需要时返回CPU内存。
notes.detail: 设备DRAM由GDDR芯片或HBM堆栈构成。结果可保留在设备内存中供后续计算使用，也可在需要时返回CPU内存。
keyPoints: 设备内存为GDDR或HBM
结果可留在设备内存复用
需要时结果返回CPU内存

notes.title: Registers and caches reduce how often execution reaches DRAM
notes.summary: 寄存器与缓存降低执行依赖较慢主存的频率，处理器附近的数据复用减少了整个存储层次上的流量。
notes.detail: 寄存器与缓存使执行更少依赖较慢的主存。靠近处理器的数据复用可减少跨存储层次的流量。
keyPoints: 寄存器与缓存减少对主存的依赖
近处理器数据复用降低层次间流量

notes.title: Deeper and larger cache hierarchies (AMD Barcelona)
notes.summary: 以2007年AMD Barcelona为例，缓存层次更深更大：私有缓存把常用数据留在各核心附近，共享缓存支持跨处理器复用。
notes.detail: 私有缓存让频繁使用的数据靠近各个核心。共享缓存则支持整个处理器范围内的数据复用。
keyPoints: 私有缓存服务单个核心
共享缓存支持跨核复用
层次更深更大

notes.title: Apple M1 cache hierarchy
notes.summary: 2020年Apple M1在芯片上为片上存储分配了大量面积，使数据靠近CPU和GPU执行资源。
notes.detail: 该芯片将相当大面积的裸片用于片上存储。这样数据能保持在CPU与GPU执行资源附近。
keyPoints: 片上存储占用大量裸片面积
数据靠近CPU与GPU执行资源

notes.title: AMD Ryzen 5000 cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3 sizing)
notes.summary: 2020年AMD Ryzen 5000有8核，每核L1为32KB、L2为512KB，共享L3为32MB；共享末级缓存可在请求到达DRAM前保留多核共用数据。
notes.detail: 每核拥有32KB L1和512KB L2，8核共享32MB L3。共享末级缓存能在请求到达DRAM之前保留多个核心使用的数据。
keyPoints: 8核，L1 32KB/核，L2 512KB/核
L3 32MB共享
共享末级缓存拦截发往DRAM的请求

notes.title: IBM POWER10 large shared L3 cache
notes.summary: IBM POWER10 (2020) has 15–16 cores, 2MB L2 per core and a 120MB shared L3, showing how large shared caches reduce main-memory traffic.
notes.detail: Cache capacity helps reduce traffic to main memory, but access time still depends on where the data sits.
keyPoints: 15–16 cores with 2MB L2 per core
120MB shared L3 cache
Capacity cuts main-memory traffic, not access latency

notes.title: Nvidia Ampere (GA102) SM-local L1 and shared L2
notes.summary: Nvidia Ampere GA102 (2020) gives each SM 128KB of L1 and shares a 6MB L2 across the device, with the A100 scaling up SMs and L2.
notes.detail: Many SMs share the device-wide L2 cache, and a larger accelerator needs more capacity and data supply.
keyPoints: 128KB L1 per SM
6MB shared L2
A100 uses the same architecture with more SMs and L2

notes.title: AMD Zen 3 enlarged L3 (32MB to 96MB)
notes.summary: AMD raised the L3 of its 8-core Zen 3 processors from 32MB to 96MB by stacking an extra 64MB L3 cache die on top of the processor die.
notes.detail: The additional 64MB L3 cache die is stacked on the processor die, bringing the total to 96MB of L3.
keyPoints: L3 grows from 32MB to 96MB
Extra 64MB L3 die stacked on the processor die
Total of 96MB L3 cache

notes.title: Apple M1 Ultra multi-level storage around compute
notes.summary: The Apple M1 Ultra system (2022) places multiple storage levels around its compute resources, balancing capacity, access time and reuse.
notes.detail: The design arranges several storage levels around the compute resources rather than relying on a single memory tier.
keyPoints: Multiple storage levels surround the compute
Balances capacity, access time and reuse
Apple M1 Ultra System, 2022

notes.title: Memory hierarchy principle: fast small memory for frequent data, large slow memory for infrequent da
notes.summary: The hierarchy puts frequent data in fast but expensive small memory such as cache, and infrequent data in slow but cheap large memory such as main memory or disk.
notes.detail: The hierarchy pays off because the working set changes over time and a small active subset receives most accesses.
keyPoints: Frequent data: fast, expensive, small memory
Infrequent data: slow, cheap, large memory
Useful when a small active subset gets most accesses

notes.title: Temporal and spatial locality
notes.summary: Temporal locality means a piece of data is quickly reused in the future, while spatial locality means neighbors of the current access tend to be accessed soon.
notes.detail: Loops exemplify temporal locality, and arrays exemplify spatial locality.
keyPoints: Temporal locality: quick reuse of the same data
Spatial locality: nearby data accessed soon after
Loops for temporal, arrays for spatial

notes.title: Locality demonstrated in loop code (reuse of variable D)
notes.summary: In the loop C[i] = A[i] * B[i] + D, D is reused every iteration (temporal locality) while A, B and C are used in sequence (spatial locality).
notes.detail: Because C[0] through C[99] are used in order, the block is fetched once and cached.
keyPoints: D reused every iteration: temporal locality
A, B, C used in sequence: spatial locality
Fetch once, cache the block

notes.title: Cache hit vs. miss and the benefit/penalty tradeoff
notes.summary: A hit means the requested block is found in the current cache level with a valid tag match; a miss means it must be retrieved from the next lower level, incurring a penalty.
notes.detail: Hit rate is hits divided by total accesses, miss rate is 1 minus hit rate, and miss penalty is the additional time a miss costs.
keyPoints: Hit: valid tag match in the current level
Miss: block retrieved from the next lower level
Miss rate = 1 − Hit rate

notes.title: Average Memory Access Time (AMAT) formula
notes.summary: AMAT equals hit time plus miss rate times miss penalty, where the miss penalty is the time to fetch a block from the lower memory level.
notes.detail: Miss penalty is the access time plus the data size divided by bandwidth. A cache helps when common hits stay fast and few accesses pay the miss penalty.
keyPoints: AMAT = Hit time + Miss rate × Miss penalty
Miss penalty = access time + data size / bandwidth
Cache helps when hits are fast and misses are few
notes.formula: \(AMAT = Hit\ time + Miss\ rate \times Miss\ penalty\)

notes.title: Memory hierarchy performance with hit time and miss penalty numbers
notes.summary: With a 1-cycle L1 hit, 10% miss rate and 300-cycle miss penalty, AMAT is 1 + 0.1 × 300 = 31 cycles.
notes.detail: The example applies AMAT = Thit(L1) + Miss%(L1) × T(memory) to a first-level cache backed by main memory.
keyPoints: Cache hit = 1 cycle
Miss rate = 10%, miss penalty = 300 cycles
AMAT = 1 + 0.1 × 300 = 31 cycles

notes.title: Multi-level caches to reduce miss penalty
notes.summary: Adding L2 and L3 caches between L1 and DRAM lowers the average memory access time because an L1 miss is usually served by a faster lower level instead of main memory.
notes.detail: The hierarchy goes L1 (1 clk), L2 (10 clks), L3 (20 clks), then DRAM (300 clks). AMAT is computed as Thit(L1) plus the miss term, which now resolves at the next level rather than at DRAM.
keyPoints: L1 hit is 1 clk, while DRAM access is 300 clks.
L2 and L3 sit on-die between L1 and main memory.
Each level absorbs misses from the level above it.

notes.title: Code optimization: blocking/tiling to improve locality
notes.summary: Traversing an array column-wise gives poor locality, while blocking (tiling) the loops so a small tile is computed at once improves locality.
notes.detail: The poor version loops over j then i and accumulates A[i][j]. The better version steps in blocks of size B and calls compute_tile on each B×B sub-block.
keyPoints: Column-wise traversal is the poor-locality baseline.
Blocking processes an N×N matrix in B×B tiles.
Tiling keeps working data close together in the cache.

notes.title: End-to-end load/store path: TLB, cache hierarchy, DRAM
notes.summary: A load or store resolves its address through the TLB, then the cache hierarchy, and only a miss all the way down sends the request to the memory controller and DRAM.
notes.detail: A TLB miss requires address translation work. A cache miss determines whether the data must come from a lower level.
keyPoints: A TLB miss triggers address translation work.
A cache miss decides whether a lower level is needed.
Only a full hierarchy miss reaches the memory controller and DRAM.

notes.title: SRAM operation (write, read, precharge)
notes.summary: An SRAM write drives the bit lines and selects the row, while a read precharges bit and bitbar to Vdd, selects the row, and uses a sense amp to detect the difference.
notes.detail: In a write, bit=1 and bitbar=0 are driven onto the bit lines before the row is selected. In a read, the cell pulls one line and the sense amp on the column detects the difference between bit and bitbar.
keyPoints: Write: drive bit lines, then select the row.
Read: precharge bit and bitbar to Vdd first.
The sense amp detects the bit/bitbar difference.

notes.title: SRAM vs. DRAM characteristics (stability, power, density)
notes.summary: SRAM stores data in a stable transistor circuit needing low power but 6 transistors per bit, whereas DRAM uses one transistor per bit with tiny capacitors, making it cheap but requiring rewrite and refresh.
notes.detail: SRAM retains a bit with low power (423mV for 45nm) and is used in caches and register files. DRAM represents a bit as charged or discharged, must be re-written after being read, and must be periodically refreshed, with each row refreshed simultaneously.
keyPoints: SRAM: 6 transistors/bit, stable, low retention power.
DRAM: 1 transistor/bit, cheap, needs rewrite and refresh.
DRAM addresses are multiplexed via RAS (row) and the lower half.

notes.title: DRAM cell operation (capacitor storage, bit lines)
notes.summary: A DRAM write drives the bit lines and selects the row, while a read precharges the bit line to Vdd and the cell shares charge with it, producing a very small voltage change that a sense amp detects.
notes.detail: The sense amp can detect changes of about 10–100k electrons. The read is destructive, so the value must be written back to restore it.
keyPoints: Read precharges the bit line to Vdd, then selects the row.
Cell and bit line share charges, giving tiny voltage changes.
The sense amp detects ~10–100k electron changes; write restores the value.

notes.title: DRAM refresh requirements for leaky storage
notes.summary: DRAM storage leaks, so every row must be periodically refreshed within 64ms by reading and writing back the same data, making the row un-accessible during refresh.
notes.detail: With 4K rows and a 100ns read cycle, one full refresh takes 4096×100ns = 410µs. That is 410µs/64ms = 0.64% unavailability.
keyPoints: Each row is refreshed within 64ms.
Refresh reads and writes back the same data.
A row is un-accessible while being refreshed.

notes.title: Why DRAM is slow: weak storage signal and sense amplification
notes.summary: DRAM is slow because tiny capacitor charges give only a small voltage difference on long bitlines, the sense amp needs time to amplify it, reads are destructive, and dense arrays add RC delay.
notes.detail: The sense amplifier must turn a very small voltage change into a full 0/1 value. Reading disturbs the stored charge, so data must be restored after every row activation, and long rows/bitlines raise RC delay.
keyPoints: Weak storage signal on long bitlines.
Sensing and amplification take time.
Destructive read requires restore; large dense arrays add RC delay.

notes.title: Multi-bank DRAM and independent bank storage
notes.summary: A multi-banked DRAM chip has independent storage arrays so work in one bank can overlap preparation in another, though the shared data bus still limits how much the channel returns at once.
notes.detail: The memory controller drives address and command over the command bus and exchanges data over the data bus of the channel. Banks provide independent storage arrays.
keyPoints: Banks are independent storage arrays.
Work in one bank overlaps preparation in another.
The shared data bus caps channel throughput.

notes.title: Multi-bank, multi-rank DIMM organization
notes.summary: A rank combines DRAM chips to match the channel data width, and multiple ranks share the channel, with the controller selecting a rank and scheduling requests across its banks.
notes.detail: The controller selects a rank and schedules requests across its banks. Multiple ranks share the channel.
keyPoints: A rank matches the channel data width.
Multiple ranks share one channel.
The controller selects a rank and schedules across its banks.

notes.title: Memory controller buffering and request scheduling
notes.summary: The memory controller buffers cache lines in both directions and schedules requests at two levels: bank and channel.
notes.detail: It holds a cache line read buffer and a cache line write buffer. Request scheduling is organized in two levels, bank and channel.
keyPoints: Buffers cache lines in both directions
Has separate read and write buffers
Schedules requests at bank and channel levels

notes.title: Memory channel organization and signal routing
notes.summary: One memory-controller port drives one channel, where command, address and clock signals select the destination and only the selected rank drives the shared data bus.
notes.detail: All ranks share the data bus, but only the selected rank may drive it. Peak bandwidth equals transfer rate times bus width divided by 8.
keyPoints: One controller port per channel
Command, address and clock signals select the destination
All ranks share the data bus; only the selected rank drives it

notes.title: Channel bandwidth scaling across channels, banks, and signaling
notes.summary: Bandwidth grows along three axes: independent channels add bandwidth when requests use them concurrently, and bank scheduling improves bus utilization.
notes.detail: DDR5 splits 64 data bits into two 32-bit subchannels, but this split alone does not double total data width.
keyPoints: Independent channels add bandwidth when used concurrently
Bank scheduling improves bus utilization
DDR5's 2x32-bit split does not double total data width

notes.title: DDR1 to DDR5 bandwidth evolution
notes.summary: At the selected upper rates, the same aggregate x64 width rises from 3.2 to 51.2 GB/s across DDR1 to DDR5.
notes.detail: Faster interfaces, longer bursts, and more bank parallelism raise throughput, while cell access improves more slowly.
keyPoints: Same x64 width goes from 3.2 to 51.2 GB/s
Faster interfaces, longer bursts and bank parallelism raise throughput
Cell access improves more slowly

topics.title: GPU Memory Hierarchy and Access Patterns

notes.title: GPU memory spaces: registers, shared memory/L1, larger capacity with longer access time
notes.summary: GPU memory spaces range from per-thread registers and per-SM shared memory/L1 to device-wide L2 and off-chip GDDR/HBM device memory.
notes.detail: Registers are allocated per thread and hardware managed, while shared memory plus L1 is a per-SM explicit scratchpad and hardware cache. L2 is device-wide and shared by all SMs, and device memory is off-chip physical memory serving the global address space.
keyPoints: Registers are per-thread and hardware managed
Shared memory + L1 is per SM
L2 is device-wide; device memory is off-chip GDDR/HBM

notes.title: Memory access traversal through SM-local storage, L2, and device DRAM
notes.summary: A memory request reaches device-wide L2 through the on-chip interconnect, and an L2 miss continues to a memory controller.
notes.detail: All SMs share L2 and the DRAM partitions, which are implemented with GDDR devices or HBM channels.
keyPoints: Requests reach L2 via the on-chip interconnect
An L2 miss continues to a memory controller
All SMs share L2 and the DRAM partitions

notes.title: Programmer's view of CUDA memories: scope and lifetime
notes.summary: Scope identifies which threads can access data, and lifetime identifies how long the data exists.
notes.detail: __syncthreads() coordinates threads within one block but does not synchronize different blocks.
keyPoints: Scope = which threads can access the data
Lifetime = how long the data exists
__syncthreads() only synchronizes within one block

notes.title: Mapping of CUDA memory spaces to physical resources
notes.summary: Every CUDA memory space maps to a physical resource, and local memory is thread-private in scope but usually resides in device DRAM.
notes.detail: Local memory passes through L1/L2. Register and shared-memory allocations limit how many blocks and warps can reside on an SM.
keyPoints: Local memory is thread-private but usually in device DRAM
Local memory passes through L1/L2
Register and shared-memory allocations limit SM residency

notes.title: Warp memory instruction generating up to 32 addresses
notes.summary: One warp memory instruction generates up to 32 addresses, which the coalescer groups by cache-sector or transaction granularity before DRAM access.
notes.detail: The transaction count depends on alignment, address spacing, access width, and GPU architecture.
keyPoints: One warp instruction generates up to 32 addresses
The coalescer groups addresses by sector/transaction granularity
Transaction count depends on alignment, spacing, width and architecture

notes.title: Memory coalescing into fewer transactions
notes.summary: Coalescing packs nearby addresses into fewer transactions and is evaluated for one warp memory instruction.
notes.detail: Aligned, contiguous addresses touch fewer segments, while misalignment can cross extra boundaries and strided accesses can touch many more segments.
keyPoints: Evaluated per warp memory instruction
Aligned, contiguous addresses touch fewer segments
Misalignment and strided accesses touch more segments

notes.title: Data layout determining useful memory bandwidth (row-wise vs. column-wise)
notes.summary: Row-wise and column-wise traversal can perform the same arithmetic while transferring different byte counts, so data layout determines useful memory bandwidth.
notes.detail: Useful bandwidth depends on requested bytes relative to the bytes actually transferred.
keyPoints: Same arithmetic, different transferred byte counts
Useful bandwidth = requested bytes vs. bytes transferred

notes.title: Shared memory as explicit on-chip data staging
notes.summary: Shared memory creates an explicit on-chip data stage where software chooses what to stage and when threads synchronize.
notes.detail: One off-chip load can support repeated on-chip reuse, reducing DRAM traffic and increasing arithmetic intensity.
keyPoints: Software explicitly chooses data to stage and sync points
One off-chip load supports repeated on-chip reuse
Reduces DRAM traffic and raises arithmetic intensity

notes.title: Shared memory bank conflicts serializing accesses
notes.summary: Typical GPUs use 32 banks; same-address reads can broadcast, but different addresses in the same bank need multiple service rounds, serializing otherwise parallel accesses.
notes.detail: This differs from global-memory coalescing. The figure shows 8 banks for readability, but real GPUs typically use 32.
keyPoints: Typical GPUs use 32 banks (figure shows 8 for readability)
Same-address reads can use broadcast
Different addresses in the same bank require multiple service rounds

notes.title: DDR DIMMs vs. GDDR: soldered devices, point-to-point links
notes.summary: GDDR uses soldered devices and short point-to-point links instead of socketed DIMMs with multiple ranks, replaceable modules, and longer routed channels.
notes.detail: Short, fixed point-to-point routes permit higher per-pin data rates, but with less expandability than socketed DIMMs.
keyPoints: Socketed DIMM: multiple ranks, replaceable modules, longer routed channel
GDDR: soldered devices with short point-to-point links
Point-to-point routes raise per-pin data rates but reduce expandability

notes.title: GDDR aggregate bandwidth from more channels and faster signaling
notes.summary: Aggregate bandwidth is the sum across independent memory-controller channels, raised by more channels, wider buses, and faster signaling.
notes.detail: These same levers also raise pin count, routing complexity, and I/O power.
keyPoints: Aggregate bandwidth sums across independent memory-controller channels
More channels, wider buses, and faster signaling raise bandwidth
Costs: higher pin count, routing complexity, and I/O power

notes.title: GDDR5 to GDDR7 signaling evolution (PAM3/PAM4)
notes.summary: GDDR6X uses PAM4 as a vendor extension, while GDDR7 uses PAM3 and further divides the channels.
notes.detail: The rates shown are representative; actual rates depend on the product and speed bin.
keyPoints: GDDR6X: PAM4 as a vendor extension
GDDR7: PAM3 plus further channel division
Shown rates are representative, depending on product and speed bin

notes.title: HBM wide interface (1024-bit, 2048-bit in HBM4)
notes.summary: HBM1–HBM3 use a 1024-bit interface per stack, and HBM4 expands the interface to 2048 bits.
notes.detail: Dense, short wiring improves bandwidth and energy per bit, while requiring advanced packaging.
keyPoints: HBM1–HBM3: 1024-bit interface per stack
HBM4: 2048-bit interface
Dense short wiring improves bandwidth and energy per bit but needs advanced packaging

notes.title: HBM overview: stacked dies and micro-bumps in one package
notes.summary: HBM places a memory stack in one package, where TSVs carry signals and power through the stack and micro-bumps connect adjacent dies.
notes.detail: More stacked dies increase capacity, and a wide channel organization increases bandwidth.
keyPoints: TSVs carry signals and power through the stack
Micro-bumps connect adjacent dies
More stacked dies raise capacity; wide channel organization raises bandwidth

notes.title: 2.5D packaging with HBM beside XPU on interposer
notes.summary: HBM commonly sits beside the XPU on an interposer, forming a 2.5D package with dense connections.
notes.detail: Dense connections improve bandwidth and energy per bit, with costs in assembly, yield, cooling, and power delivery.
keyPoints: HBM sits beside the XPU on an interposer (2.5D package)
Dense connections improve bandwidth and energy per bit
Costs: assembly, yield, cooling, and power delivery

notes.title: HBM1 to HBM4 scaling via signaling, stack height, and interface width
notes.summary: HBM scales through faster signaling, greater stack height, and the wider HBM4 interface.
notes.detail: Per-stack figures are representative; package space, thermal limits, and yield constrain stack count and height.
keyPoints: Scaling levers: faster signaling, greater stack height, wider HBM4 interface
Per-stack figures are representative
Package space, thermal limits, and yield constrain stacks

notes.title: DDR, GDDR, and HBM optimizing different constraints
notes.summary: DDR favors capacity, expandability, and cost per GB; GDDR balances pin bandwidth and board cost; HBM favors bandwidth per package and per watt.
notes.detail: The choice depends on the workload and system constraints.
keyPoints: DDR: capacity, expandability, cost per GB
GDDR: balance of pin bandwidth and board cost
HBM: bandwidth per package and per watt

notes.title: Banked LLC logically shared but physically distributed with address hashing
notes.summary: A banked LLC is logically shared but physically distributed, with a physical-address hash selecting a home LLC slice.
notes.detail: Reads and writes to remote slices would slow down memory access speed.
keyPoints: Logically shared, physically distributed LLC
Physical-address hash selects the home LLC slice
Remote-slice reads/writes would slow memory access

notes.title: LLC serving repeated reads without reaching DRAM
notes.summary: Only the first cold read must reach DRAM; a second reader can obtain the line from the LLC or the current owner.
notes.detail: This is a simplified inclusive teaching model; modern LLCs may also be non-inclusive.
keyPoints: Only the first cold read reaches DRAM
A second reader gets the line from the LLC or current owner
Simplified inclusive teaching model; modern LLCs may be non-inclusive

notes.title: Coherence problem: writes making other cores' copies stale
notes.summary: A write can make another core's copy stale, so coherence requires write propagation and write serialization.
notes.detail: Write propagation means other processors must eventually observe the write; write serialization means all processors must agree on one order for writes to the same location.
keyPoints: A write can make another core's copy stale
Write propagation: others must eventually observe the write
Write serialization: all processors agree on one write order

notes.title: Snooping vs. directory coherence protocols
notes.summary: Snooping broadcasts coherence requests, while a directory tracks owners and sharers to target messages; MESI describes permissions, and the design choice determines how coherence messages reach caches.
notes.detail: Snooping and directory designs differ in how coherence messages are delivered. MESI describes permissions, but the protocol design determines the message delivery mechanism.
keyPoints: Snooping broadcasts coherence requests to caches.
A directory tracks owners and sharers to target messages.
MESI describes permissions, not message delivery.

notes.title: Capacity wall of LLM inference: KV-cache size case study (DeepSeek, GB200)
notes.summary: With ~150GB of HBM available for KV-cache on a GB200 GPU, DeepSeek v3.2 holds only ~4 sessions at 1M context, showing HBM can hold limited KV-cache and the GPU is much underutilized.
notes.detail: KV-cache size grows with context length: DeepSeek v3.2 needs ~5.72 GiB at 128K and ~45.75 GiB at 1M, while DeepSeek v4 (with CSA/HCA/SWA) needs ~0.62 GiB and ~4.83 GiB respectively. At 1M context, a GPU holds ~4 sessions for v3.2 and ~32 for v4pro.
keyPoints: Available HBM capacity for KV-cache is ~150GB.
At 1M context, DeepSeek v3.2 holds ~4 sessions; v4pro ~32.
The capacity wall leaves the GPU much underutilized.

notes.title: CXL memory extension and unified host address map
notes.summary: CXL provides a unified host address map across host DRAM/HBM and CXL HDM, so software sees host-memory ranges while hardware translates load/store instructions into CXL remote memory accesses.
notes.detail: The unified memory spans host DRAM/HBM and CXL HDM. Software operates on host-memory ranges, and hardware handles translation of load/store instructions into remote CXL accesses.
keyPoints: Unified memory covers host DRAM/HBM and CXL HDM.
Software sees host-memory ranges.
Hardware translates load/store into CXL remote accesses.

notes.title: CXL switches enabling expansion, pooling, and sharing
notes.summary: CXL switches support expansion (adding capacity to one host) and pooling (assigning portions of memory devices to different hosts), while CXL 3.0 coherent sharing goes beyond merely mapping the same region on several hosts.
notes.detail: Expansion adds capacity to a single host, whereas pooling assigns portions of memory devices to different hosts. CXL 3.0 coherent sharing differs from simply allowing several hosts to map the same memory region.
keyPoints: Expansion adds capacity to one host.
Pooling assigns memory device portions to different hosts.
CXL 3.0 coherent sharing differs from shared mapping.

notes.title: LPDDR memory extension via coherent NVLink-C2C (Grace-Hopper)
notes.summary: Hopper keeps local HBM while Grace connects LPDDR5X through the coherent NVLink-C2C CPU–GPU link, extending the capacity the accelerator can address without enlarging HBM itself.
notes.detail: The LPDDR tier is reached over the coherent NVLink-C2C link between Grace CPU and Hopper GPU. This extends addressable capacity but does not enlarge HBM.
keyPoints: Hopper retains local HBM.
Grace connects LPDDR5X via coherent NVLink-C2C.
LPDDR extends addressable capacity, not HBM size.

notes.title: Tiered memory management deciding what stays in HBM
notes.summary: Tiered memory management keeps hot, latency-critical, frequently reused data in HBM and places large, cold objects in the LPDDR capacity tier, promoting only when future reuse outweighs transfer and bookkeeping cost.
notes.detail: Placement decisions separate hot, latency-critical data (HBM) from large, cold objects (LPDDR tier). Promotion is worthwhile only when future reuse saves more than the transfer and bookkeeping cost.
keyPoints: Keep hot, latency-critical, frequently reused data in HBM.
Place large, cold objects in the LPDDR capacity tier.
Promotion pays off only if reuse exceeds transfer and bookkeeping cost.

  restored after every row activation.
  Large dense arrays
 DRAM prioritizes capacity and cost per bit, so rows/bitlines are long and
  have higher RC delay.
  Solution: Multi-Bank, Multi-Rank DRAM

Multicore Technologies: Coherence
  Coherence Protocols: Snooping and Directory





▪ Snooping broadcasts coherence requests. A directory tracks owners and sharers
  to target the messages.
▪ MESI describes permissions. Snooping and directory designs determine how
  coherence messages reach the caches.

SOTA Memory Technologies

CXL Switches Enable Expansion, Pooling, and Sharing





▪ Expansion adds capacity to one host. Pooling assigns portions of memory devices
  to different hosts.
▪ CXL 3.0 coherent sharing differs from merely allowing several hosts to map the
 same memory region.

sources.68:
SOTA Memory Technologies

Memory Extension: LPDDR





▪ Hopper retains local HBM. Grace connects LPDDR5X through the coherent
  NVLink-C2C CPU–GPU link.
▪ LPDDR extends the capacity the accelerator can address; it does not enlarge
 HBM itself.

sources.69:
SOTA Memory Technologies

Tiered Memory Management Decides What Stays in HBM





▪ Keep hot, latency-critical, frequently reused data in HBM. Place large, cold objects
  in the LPDDR capacity tier.
▪ Promotion helps only when future reuse saves more than the transfer and
  bookkeeping cost.
